Trademark Assignment & Licence Recordal in China: Getting Your Mark Back from a Factory

A foreign company can own a Chinese trademark, an application under examination can be assigned, and a signed assignment statement is usually all the transfer needs. The 2026 law adds one important new caveat.

Four Myths That Keep Brands Stuck

When a factory, distributor or former agent has registered the mark, the counterparty often insists that a transfer is impossible. International practitioners consistently report the same four claims — and none of them is correct:

  1. "Only Chinese entities can own a Chinese trademark." Foreign companies own a large number of Chinese registrations. There is no nationality restriction on ownership.
  2. "The only route is to abandon the mark and refile." That is costly, slow and exposes a gap in which a third party can file. The normal route is a filed assignment.
  3. "An application under examination cannot be assigned." It can — although if the application is later refused, the assignee receives nothing.
  4. "Both parties need consular-certified corporate documents." Identity evidence is required for both assignor and assignee, but a trademark assignment does not generally require embassy legalisation of those documents.

The transfer itself is typically documented by an assignment statement filed with CNIPA together with identity evidence. The hard part is usually commercial — negotiating the terms with the holder — not procedural. See also the four recovery options.

The 2026 Caveat: Transfers Are No Longer Purely Formal

Article 46 of the revised Trademark Law retains the assignment rule and adds a third paragraph: a transfer that is likely to cause confusion or has other adverse effects shall not be approved. That is a substantive review layer which did not appear in the 2019 provision.

For a brand buying back a squatted mark, this means the assignment document should do more than say "transferred". It should explain the relationship between the parties, the business rationale, what happens to related or similar marks held by the assignor, and how the goods and channels will be separated so that consumers are not confused. Where the holder owns a family of lookalike marks, the agreement should require assignment or cancellation of the whole family rather than just the one mark you noticed.

Article 47 adds a parallel rule for collective and certification marks: the assignee must have the relevant qualifications and supervisory capacity. Article 53 also matters in dispute planning — an invalidation generally has no retroactive effect on assignment or licence contracts already performed, except where the registrant acted in bad faith.

Licence Recordal and What It Actually Does

ItemRule under the 2026 law (Art. 55)
Quality controlThe licensor must supervise the quality of the licensee's goods; the licensee must guarantee that quality
Statutory terminationIf the licensee fails to meet its quality obligations, the licensor may terminate the licence — a statutory right that does not depend on a termination clause being written into the contract
MarkingGoods bearing a licensed mark must indicate the licensee's name and the place of origin
RecordalThe licence must be filed with the trademark authority and published; an unrecorded licence cannot be asserted against a bona fide third party

Recordal is therefore not a formality: it is what makes the licensee's position defensible against third parties, and it is frequently requested by platform IP portals when a licensee rather than the brand owner operates the store. It also creates the documented licence relationship needed if the licensee's sales are later relied on as use evidence against a non-use cancellation.

Licence structures are commonly described as exclusive, sole or non-exclusive. Whichever is used, define territory, duration, goods, sub-licensing, quality inspection rights, audit rights, what happens to stock and packaging on termination, and dispute resolution.

Assignment, Licence, Invalidation or Refiling?

RouteWhen it fitsMain trade-off
Assignment / buy-backThe holder is identifiable and willing to deal; launch date is fixedFastest, but rewards the behaviour and needs Article 46-ready documentation
Licence + recordalYou need immediate market access while ownership is disputedDoes not give you ownership; recordal and quality terms are essential
Invalidation / oppositionBad faith and prior rights are well evidenced; no urgencyStrongest legal outcome, longest timeline
Filing a new, distinct markThe original mark is commercially expendableRebranding cost; the old mark remains with the squatter

Preventing the Problem in the OEM Relationship

  • File in China before disclosing the brand, packaging or product roadmap to a factory or distributor.
  • Put an express no-self-registration clause in the manufacturing agreement, with a duty to assign anything filed and a meaningful liquidated damages figure.
  • Allocate end-of-term stock, moulds, semi-finished goods and packaging — each category needs its own disposal rule and deadline.
  • Define authorised production volume, reconciliation duties and audit rights; a presumption against the factory for unexplained units is more useful than a general promise.
  • Keep the licence and assignment documentation consistent with the goods actually registered, and record changes of name, address and agent promptly (Art. 57 imposes penalties for uncorrected changes to registered particulars).

Sources and Caveats

Primary sources: Articles 46, 47, 53, 55 and 57 of the Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision) (CNIPA, 26 June 2026) and CNIPA Main Contents of the Revision (10 July 2026); practitioner guidance on assignments of Chinese trademarks to foreign entities and OEM agreement clauses. Document requirements and examination practice may be refined by the revised Implementing Regulations. This is general information, not legal advice; a live dispute needs advice on its specific facts.
